title: Fregolata
subtitle: crumbly Venetian almond tart with a biscuity texture
excerpt: Fregolata is a Venetian almond and polenta tart with a texture closer to a giant crumbly biscuit than a pastry case. You get a sandy, fragrant slice that shatters when you break it. Watch the colour: this thin tart goes from pale to over-baked in about 3 minutes, so check early.
sourceNotes: Fregolata is a traditional Venetian biscuit-tart, documented in regional Italian baking literature. The name comes from the Venetian dialect word for crumbs (briciole in standard Italian). It is a standard preparation of the Veneto region and appears in Italian regional cookery references.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely, wrap the whole tart or individual portions in cling film, and freeze for up to 2 months. Defrost at room temperature for 1 hour.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps well in an airtight tin for up to 5 days at room temperature. The texture actually improves slightly on the second day as the crumb firms.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 170 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 155 degrees Celsius. Check at 25 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Any pastry with a high fat-to-flour ratio that produces a crumbly, tender texture with little elasticity. The fat coats the flour particles and limits gluten development, which is what makes the pastry short (fragile and crumbly) rather than tough. Fregolata is an extreme example: it is pressed into a tin as a crumb rather than rolled, and sets into a biscuity slab.

Ground dried maize (cornmeal). In baking it adds a slightly gritty, sandy texture and a pale golden colour. Coarse polenta gives more bite; fine polenta is closer to cornflour. In fregolata, a medium-ground polenta provides the characteristic slightly rough texture that distinguishes it from a standard almond tart.

content.text: Fregolata is a Venetian almond tart. It is very high in butter and ground almonds, pressed into the tin as a crumb, and baked into a fragile slab. It is an extreme example of
gives it a sandy, gritty texture.
It shatters rather than slices. The flavour is buttery and almond, with a lemony edge and a gritty bite from the polenta.
Watch the colour during baking. Fregolata goes from done to over-baked in about 3 minutes. Start checking at 25 minutes, not 30.
Heat the oven to 170 degrees Celsius (conventional). Butter a 23 cm loose-bottomed tart tin and line the base with a circle of baking parchment.

Combine the plain flour, ground almonds, polenta, caster sugar, and salt in a large bowl. Add the cold cubed butter. Using your fingertips, rub the butter into the dry ingredients until the mixture resembles coarse, irregular crumbs with some pea-sized pieces of butter still visible. Work quickly to keep the butter cold. You are not trying to make a smooth dough: uneven crumbs are correct.

Add the egg, vanilla extract, and lemon zest. Mix briefly with a fork until the crumbs start to clump together. Stop as soon as the mixture begins to hold when squeezed. Do not work it into a dough: the goal is a crumbly mixture that just coheres when pressed, not a uniform paste.

Tip the crumb mixture into the prepared tart tin. Using your fingers, press it out evenly across the base and about 1.5 cm up the sides. The layer should be even and compact, but press only enough to make it hold together: over-pressing removes all the crumbly texture. Aim for about 1 cm thickness across the base.
If using, scatter flaked almonds across the top and press them in very lightly.

Bake for 25 to 30 minutes. Check at 25 minutes: the tart should be golden across the surface and the edges should have pulled away slightly from the sides of the tin. The centre may look very slightly underdone; it will firm as it cools. If the edges are darkening faster than the centre, cover loosely with foil and return to the oven for 5 minutes.

Remove from the oven and leave the fregolata to cool completely in the tin before attempting to unmould. This is not optional: fregolata is fragile when warm and will break apart if moved before it has set. Set the tin on a cooling rack and leave for at least 1 hour.

Once completely cool, place the tin on a can or upturned glass and gently push the base down to release the tart. Slide it off the base onto a board or plate. Fregolata is traditionally served broken into irregular shards rather than sliced into neat portions, but it can also be cut with a sharp knife if you prefer even pieces. Dust with icing sugar to serve.

attrs.problem: The fregolata broke apart when unmoulding
attrs.avoid: Avoid unmoulding before the tart is completely cold. The crumb structure sets fully only once the butter has re-solidified.
attrs.fix: If it has broken into a few large pieces, press them gently back together on the board: the butter will hold them as long as the pieces are still at room temperature. Serve broken into shards and present it as intentional.

attrs.problem: The texture is dense and heavy rather than crumbly and sandy
attrs.avoid: Avoid overworking the mixture once the egg is added. Excess mixing develops gluten and binds the crumbs into a tough paste.
attrs.fix: The butter may also have been too warm when rubbed in. Keep it cold and work quickly with your fingertips. If your hands are warm, use a food processor to pulse the butter into the dry ingredients instead.

attrs.problem: The top is over-dark at the edges before the centre is cooked
attrs.avoid: Avoid using a dark-coloured tin, which absorbs more heat and browns the edges faster than a lighter tin.
attrs.fix: Cover the edges loosely with a strip of foil and return to the oven until the centre looks set and golden. Reduce the oven temperature by 10 degrees Celsius next time.
